text: Version 4 of the workflow engine design is issued as Draft. No approval of the source version and no approval of this version is recorded in any source read by this work package.
why: The run records no human approval; a missing approval is treated as an assumption and the document continues in Draft rather than stopping.
read: Template and Rules v1 R8.1 and the realignment overlay D-RCV-60 (missing status is an assumption, not a stop).
applied_in: Metadata table, Status row; section 8 delivery table
confirm: The document owner confirms or records the approval of version 4.
impact: Documentation only; nothing is built from an unapproved status.

text: Quartz is retired in the target design: the Epic 1-2 column of version 3 is restated as durable timers in the owning service, and JOB-05 keeps no Schedule. The past behaviour of Quartz is described as retired rather than kept.
why: The rules retire TE-007 (Quartz scheduler replaced by Temporal Schedules in RWB-PLT-E1071) and ADR-016 replaces Quartz with Schedules; the design document therefore cannot keep Quartz as the target for Epics 1-2.
read: Template and Rules v1 R6 (TE-007 retired, dependencies point to RWB-PLT-E1071-CON); ids.json ADR-016; Architecture v5 slide 44 JOB-05 'durable timers (retired)' and slide 5 'Business schedules run as Temporal Schedules in the owning service'.
confirm: The platform team confirms that no Epic 1-2 job stays on Quartz in the target.
impact: Every timer and every job in sections 4 and 5.1 is a Temporal construct; no qrtz_* table is used.

text: rwb-platform is the task queue of the platform team for the platform workflows and Schedules (JOB-21, JOB-22 and PlatformSmokeWorkflow). It is not one of the 19 service queues and has no schema or REST base of its own.
why: Version 3 names rwb-platform as a queue, the Architecture v5 job map gives JOB-21 and JOB-22 to the platform, and no service row exists for it; the queue is kept so the two platform jobs have an owner and a queue.
read: Workflow Engine Design v3 section 5 Task queues; Architecture v5 slide 44 JOB-21 and JOB-22 (owner platform); Batch and Scheduling Design v4 JOB-22 (task queue rwb-platform); Microservice Ownership Map v1 Jobs and Workflows sheets.
applied_in: Section 5 Task queues and Workflow IDs; section 5.1 rows JOB-21 and JOB-22; section 7
confirm: The platform team confirms the queue name and that it needs no schema.
impact: One extra queue in namespace rwb-recovery, owned by RWB-PLT-WF.

text: Every business time in this design is Asia/Bangkok, and a Schedule carries its job ID as its name, no overlap, no catch-up after downtime and no pause on failure until the Schedule attributes are settled.
why: The job map gives times without a zone and no source gives the Schedule attributes; the zone comes from the Batch and Scheduling Design v4 and the rest is the safest reading that changes no business rule.
read: Architecture v5 slide 44 (times only); Batch and Scheduling Design v4 Jobs sheet ('Times are Asia/Bangkok'); Workflow Engine Design v3 (no Schedules).
confirm: The platform team and the owning services confirm the four Schedule attributes and the zone.
impact: Nine Schedules; a missed run after downtime is not caught up until the attribute is agreed.

text: The workflow kit is owned by the platform team and delivered with RWB-PLT-E1071 (epic RWB-PLT-WF), which is the contract that DP-10 makes every Schedule and kit user depend on. Its version number and artefact coordinates are left to the build.
why: R5.5 DP-10 points every Schedules story at RWB-PLT-E1071-CON, Architecture v5 slide 23 gives the kit to the platform team, and no source states a kit version.
read: Architecture v5 slide 23 (L3 workflow kit, platform team, semantic versioning); Template and Rules v1 R5.1 (RWB-PLT-WF) and R5.5 DP-10; Microservice Ownership Map v1 (no kit row).
confirm: The platform team confirms the kit owner, the story and the first version.
impact: Every stage story depends on one platform contract instead of writing its own templates.

text: The parent generates the child and kit workflow IDs from the case ID and the stage, and no source fixes that format; the document therefore keeps only case-{caseId} as a fixed ID and records the child format as an open point.
why: Architecture v5 describes the children and the kit workflows but gives no ID format, and R9 forbids inventing one in the document.
read: Workflow Engine Design v3 section 5 Workflow IDs (case-{caseId}); Architecture v5 slide 25; Temporal and Drools Design v1 slide 13.
confirm: The case service owner confirms the child ID format before Epic 3 builds the first child.
impact: Search, the run book and the reset action address a child by its ID; the parent ID is unaffected.

text: The decision record is written locally in the same transaction as the state change and sealed centrally in rwb-decision, and a point of no return waits for the ledger acknowledgement (strict mode). The wait itself is not defined in this document.
why: Architecture v5 slide 28 changes ADR-009 to a local record plus a central ledger with strict mode at the pivots; version 3 has the central log as the synchronous gate and cannot be kept as written.
read: Architecture v5 slide 28 (record locally, seal centrally, strict mode); ids.json ADR-022; Temporal and Drools Design v1 slide 16 (the record fields) and slide 26 (the pivots).
confirm: RW-RISK and Internal Audit confirm the strict-mode wait and its timeout.
impact: Debt transfer, write-off posting, auction sale and title transfer wait on the ledger; every other step runs at full speed.

text: The parent CaseWorkflow forwards each event to the running stage child and keeps no case field of its own; the stage child applies the state through the P3 case state service. 'The workflow is the only writer of case state' in version 3 is read as the case workflows of P3 and the stage services, through that service.
why: One workflow per case became a parent with a child per stage, and the case table and the CMMN state stay owned by P3 (Architecture v5 slide 41 and the Ownership Map).
read: Architecture v5 slide 25 (the parent and the children); slide 41 (P3 owns case, CMMN state, queues, tasks, allocation, timers); Microservice Ownership Map v1 Tables sheet (recovery_case and task rows to P3).
confirm: The case service owner confirms that no stage writes the case tables directly.
impact: One writer of case state; a stage writes only its own schema.

text: A deviation pauses the stage clock of the running stage child: the parent forwards DeviationRaised and DeviationCleared and the child pauses and resumes its own stage timer. The prescription clock is never paused.
why: Architecture v5 says the CaseWorkflow pauses the stage clock while the stage timer sits in the child; pausing the timer where it is held keeps one owner per clock and matches R-DEV-01.
read: Architecture v5 slide 25 notes; Temporal and Drools Design v1 slide 24 notes (EV-06 and EV-07 to the CaseWorkflow); Workflow Engine Design v3 section 4.
confirm: The case and deviation owners confirm which workflow holds and pauses the stage clock.
impact: A resume returns to the exact paused state; the legal clock keeps running.

text: The durable timer is authoritative and the timer row in rwb_case is its audit copy, written by ApplyStateActivity in the same transaction as the state and read back when a workflow reopens.
why: The timer table (E1-028) stays a P3 object and JOB-05 retires, so one of the two has to be named authoritative; a durable timer is the only one that survives a restart without a polling job.
read: Workflow Engine Design v3 section 4 (timer table E1-028, TimerScheduler four methods); Architecture v5 slide 44 JOB-05 (durable timers); Microservice Ownership Map v1 Tables sheet (timer rows to P3).
confirm: The case service owner confirms the audit-copy role of the timer row.
impact: One write path for a due date; the timer row still answers a screen query.

text: A Continue-As-New runs at a stage end only, and an event that arrives while it runs is carried into the new run by the parent rather than lost. The mechanism is left to the build.
why: Architecture v5 requires Continue-As-New at every stage end and at least every 28 days and no source states what happens to an in-flight signal.
read: Architecture v5 slide 25 notes (Continue-As-New, ABANDON); Temporal and Drools Design v1 slide 13 notes and slide 27.
confirm: The platform team confirms the Continue-As-New trigger and the in-flight signal rule.
impact: No event is lost at a history cut; a case is never half-moved.

text: The parent retries a failed child workflow start with the same workflow ID and raises an incident with MSG-P3-037 when the retries are exhausted; the case stays in its last applied state. The child timeouts are left to the build.
why: A child per stage needs a failure path, and no source gives one; the retry-then-incident pattern is the one already used for activities and for a stuck workflow.
read: Workflow Engine Design v3 section 7 (retry policy and the stuck alert); Architecture v5 slide 25 (children); Batch and Scheduling Design v4 JOB-21 (stuck workflow scan).
confirm: The case and stage owners confirm the child timeouts and the incident path.
impact: A failed child is visible in the Temporal Web UI and on the E2-037 alert.
